text.p: Here are highlights from Polish newspapers this morning.
- Opposition Republican League activists tried to stop President Aleksander Kwasniewski from entering Warsaw ceremonies launching the academic year.

- On September 30 Poland paid London Club creditors $215 million. Within less than two weeks it will have to repay $180 million to the Paris Club. Despite the reductions Poland still owes $34 billion.
- Swedish furniture firm IKEA said by the year 2000 it will invest $75 million in Poland, doubling its investment so far.

- Bydgoszcz confectioner Jutrzenka plans to increase production and is seeking ties with western firms or foreign investors. Among interested companies are two international corporations which are not yet making confectionery in Poland.

- A decision will be made within days on what vodka to produce at the Polmos plant in Zyrardow. Production will be based on Finnish technology as Primalco, maker of Finlandia vodka, has made a capital investment. The first products of the Polmos-Primalco joint venture will reach shops early next year.

- The international consortium which will advise Poland on privatisation of the KGHM copper combine expects the domestic and foreign public offers of KGHM shares to be made at the end of the second quarter of 1997. Up to 15 percent of shares will be given to employees while the issues will total 34 percent, with the state treasury retaining 51 percent.

- A Nowa Europa survey shows the appointment of Peasant politician Miroslaw Pietrewicz to head the new treasury ministry could slow privatisation as his party is not keen on this or on foreign capital. The new minister is also little known in international financial circles.

- The securities commission has received a first simplified prospectus from a machine tool maker Rafamet SA in Kuznia Raciborska. Rafamet, which also applied to be admitted to public trading, wants to launch its shares on the CeTO over-the-counter market.

- The construction of German carmaker Opel's factory in a special economic zone in Gliwice will be ceremonially launched on Wednesday. The investment totals 450 million marks and the first vehicles will leave the assembly line in 1998.

- Wprost weekly says President Kwasniewski has been helping private U.S. firm GTECH which is interested in prolonging its agreement with the Polish sports lottery company. It says Kwasniewski used GTECH aircraft during two U.S. trips.

- The Krakow prosecutor's office accused former privatisation minister Janusz Lewandowski of choosing the worst bidders during the privatisations of the Krakchemia and Techma companies. Lewandowski denies any wrongdoing.
